title: Produce, don't possess
hook: the Tao gives birth and nourishes, but doesn't possess (Tao Te Ching 51)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was no place for the tiger: claws need a handhold. Your line was no place for claws.

A parent at the curb on the first day of school waves, and then drives away. A week of chapters ends today, and under all of them runs one quiet thread: less grabbing. Great skill that looks clumsy. Knowing what is enough. Knowing the world without going out the door. Subtracting a little each day. A mind with no fixed position. A traveler with no handhold for the tiger. Chapter fifty-one takes that thread to the very source of things, and asks what the Tao itself does with everything it brings to life. The answer sounds a lot like that wave at the curb.
screen: `A WAVE AT THE CURB.` → `A WEEK OF LESS GRABBING.` → `WHAT DOES THE SOURCE DO?`

segments.voice: First, the making. All things come from the Tao, the chapter says, and are nourished by its virtue, its power, the Te in Tao Te Ching. Then they take shape and are brought to completion. Things grow, in this picture, because something gives and keeps on giving. Second, the honor. Everything honors the Tao, but not because anyone ordered it to. Nobody issues a decree. The respect simply arises, the way people come to trust a well that has never run dry. Third, the line that gives today its title. In James Legge's translation: "It produces them and makes no claim to the possession of them." And it keeps going in the same rhythm. It carries things along and doesn't boast. It brings them to maturity and doesn't control them. The chapter calls this the mysterious virtue. The source gives life, and then lets go of what it gave life to. Fourth, closer to home. Making something and wanting to own it can arrive as a single motion. The project with your name on it. The kid who should turn out the way you planned. The friend you helped, who ought to remember. The chapter doesn't say stop making, stop raising, stop helping. It says do all of it, fully, and then don't hold the deed. A garden grows better when the gardener stops pulling up the seedlings to check the roots.
screen: `ALL THINGS COME FROM THE TAO.` · `HONORED WITHOUT ANY DECREE.` · `IT PRODUCES, AND DOESN'T POSSESS.` · `MAKE IT FULLY, THEN DON'T HOLD THE DEED.` · then, large: `THE MYSTERIOUS VIRTUE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've helped along lately: a plant, a project, a younger colleague, a child. See it as it is now, a little further on than before, and notice any wish to steer it, to be thanked, to have it turn out your way. You don't have to push that wish away; just set it down beside you for these two minutes, and let the thing you helped be its own.
Produce. In chapter fifty-one, the Tao produces all things and makes no claim to own them. It gives life, and doesn't grab what it gave. Today's word.
Your line: don't possess. Full giving, then open hands, the way the source does it. That's the week.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-one as a model for parents, teachers and leaders: give fully, nourish, and then let what you helped become its own.

chat.says: If I helped make something, isn't it mine to steer?
options: Chapter fifty-one says the Tao produces things and makes no claim to own them.
Yes; the chapter says whoever makes a thing should keep control of it.
No; it says never make or help anything, so nothing can be lost.
